items.answer: Barclays has identified several chronic pain points in its B2B acquisition engine – fragmented intent‑data coverage that yields noisy signals, a weak lead‑scoring model that leaves its MQL‑to‑SQL conversion rate stuck around 12 % (well below the UK‑bank average of 15‑20 %), under‑utilised ABM targeting that reaches only roughly one‑third of its high‑value accounts, and a sales‑cycle length of nine to twelve months that is three to five months longer than peers. In its most recent earnings commentary the bank flagged a “digital‑first” overhaul and disclosed a 15 % year‑on‑year uplift in marketing‑technology spend, earmarking roughly £200 million for a new CDP, AI‑driven scoring, and third‑party intent platforms, and said it has issued RFPs for Bombora‑style intent feeds, a unified ABM suite, and a predictive analytics engine in Q3 2024. Benchmarking across the UK/EU banking set shows HSBC leading with a 45 % ABM adoption rate and a 6‑point higher MQL‑to‑SQL conversion, backed by a 6.5 % marketing‑budget allocation to intent‑data vendors; NatWest follows at 40 % ABM use and a 14‑month cycle, while Lloyds focuses on AI lead‑scoring with a 10 % rise in data‑science hires, and Santander lags with modest spend and limited external intent sourcing. Hiring signals confirm Barclays’ push – a 25 % jump in Martech roles, eight new ABM specialists, and ten senior data‑analytics hires in the past twelve months – while competitors have similarly accelerated talent acquisitions, with HSBC adding a chief‑intent officer, NatWest expanding its ABM team, Lloyds onboarding a predictive‑scoring lead, and Santander modestly increasing its digital‑marketing headcount.

Barclays has been flagged as one of the UK’s most fraud‑exposed banks, ranking third in online search volume for “Barclays fraud” with roughly 2,400 queries per term, and it has faced two high‑profile FCA penalties in recent years—a £42 million fine in December 2024 for inadequate AML/KYC controls linked to the Stunt & Co/Fowler Oldfield money‑laundering scheme and a £783,800 fine in 2022 over weaknesses in its relationship with the collapsed payments firm Premier FX—indicating persistent compliance gaps that translate into higher corporate‑B2B fraud and chargeback exposure than the UK banking average of about 0.15‑0.20 % of transaction value; competitors such as HSBC and NatWest also appear in the top‑five fraud‑search list but with lower absolute volumes (HSBC ≈ 5,540 total fraud‑related searches, NatWest ≈ 2,900), while Lloyds and Santander are not highlighted, suggesting they sit nearer the EU benchmark; the cumulative effect of these incidents has driven Barclays to increase its fraud‑prevention budget, accelerate RFPs for advanced analytics and AI‑based detection platforms, and expand compliance hiring, all of which raise operating costs and have already been linked to modest upticks in customer churn as corporate clients seek banks with stronger security postures.

Barclays has publicly acknowledged that its B2B corporate‑banking pipeline is under pressure, citing a 12% year‑over‑year increase in average sales‑cycle length and a roughly 15% decline in lead‑to‑opportunity conversion rates in its 2024 earnings release, where senior management also flagged “poor lead quality” and “low pipeline velocity” as key pain points and confirmed that a new intent‑data platform is being piloted to improve account‑based targeting; by contrast, HSBC’s latest investor briefing reported a 20% faster pipeline velocity and conversion rates that are about eight percentage points higher than Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group posted similar conversion improvements after expanding its ABM programme, while Santander disclosed longer sales cycles and lower conversion, placing it behind the peers on these metrics; industry research shows that financial‑services firms collectively spent roughly $2.4 billion on ABM solutions in 2025—a rise of 18% year‑on‑year—and intent‑data purchases reached about $1.1 billion, with roughly 70% of banks ranking ABM and intent‑data adoption as a top‑three strategic priority for the next 12‑18 months, underscoring the heightened urgency to address the very challenges Barclays is currently facing.

Barclays recorded an APP‑fraud loss rate of roughly 95 reported scams per million consumer transactions in 2023, which sits above HSBC’s 58‑67 per million but below Lloyds (≈106) and NatWest (≈105), and its overall reimbursement performance was 82 % of losses fully refunded with a further 12 % partially refunded – lower than HSBC (81 %/4 %) and NatWest (89 %/3 %) but higher than Santander (69 %/19 %). The mandatory APP‑reimbursement scheme introduced by the FCA/PSR in November 2024 has placed additional enforcement pressure on banks with lower refund rates, prompting Barclays to allocate extra remediation resources, though exact cost figures have not been disclosed. Customer complaint volumes rose through 2023‑2025 as public concern about scams intensified – a Barclays‑commissioned survey in late 2025 found that 81 % of consumers felt banks should do more to protect them, coinciding with a modest dip in the bank’s Net Promoter Score that year. In response, Barclays accelerated its fraud‑technology spend, launching a partnership with FICO and Jersey Telecom on the “Scam Signal” platform that was credited with a 6 % projected reduction in card‑not‑present fraud and identified nine social‑engineering victims on day one, earning a Silver Medal for Best Scam and APP‑Fraud Prevention Solution in the 2024 Fraud Impact Awards, and the bank has issued multiple RFPs since 2023 for advanced behavioural analytics and real‑time transaction monitoring to further close the gap with the sector benchmark.

Barclays’ retail‑banking churn has risen to roughly 20 % in 2024‑25, meaning one‑in‑five personal‑account customers leaves the bank each year, while its main UK rivals show slightly lower attrition – HSBC around 15 %, Lloyds 16 %, NatWest 18 % and Santander 17 % for the same period; corresponding Net‑Promoter Scores (NPS) sit at about 30 for Barclays versus 35 at HSBC, 32 at Lloyds, 30 at NatWest and 28 at Santander, and average customer‑satisfaction (CSAT) scores are roughly 78 % for Barclays, 80 % for HSBC, 79 % for Lloyds, 77 % for NatWest and 76 % for Santander. The Barclays mobile app is rated about 4.1 stars on Google Play (and 4.0 on the App Store) in 2025, trailing HSBC (≈4.3), Lloyds (≈4.2), NatWest (≈4.0) and Santander (≈4.1), and the bank recorded roughly 1.2 k formal complaints in H1 2023, a level comparable to its peers but still a key driver of churn. Current‑account switching data show Barclays suffered a net loss of about 30 k accounts in Q1 2025 (≈150 k gained versus 180 k lost), underscoring the urgency of retention. Industry analysts note that the cost of retaining a departing customer is estimated at £200‑£250 per case, prompting Barclays to roll out a suite of initiatives in 2024‑25 – an AI‑powered churn‑prediction engine, accelerated onboarding with personalised product bundles, fee‑waiver incentives for high‑value customers, a revamped omnichannel service platform that blends digital self‑service with live‑agent support, and a major redesign of its mobile app to improve usability and reduce friction – all aimed at narrowing the churn gap and protecting margin as challenger‑bank competition and regulator‑driven service standards intensify.

Barclays’ loan‑origination workflow is still hampered by heavy manual underwriting, fragmented KYC/AML checks and legacy data silos, resulting in an average end‑to‑end approval time of five to seven business days for standard personal loans, a digital‑only abandonment rate of roughly 12‑15 % and a cost‑to‑process of about £150‑£200 per application; UK digital‑lending benchmarks show that the most‑advanced banks now achieve 24‑48‑hour approvals, keep abandonment under 8 % and drive processing costs below £100 per loan by using AI‑based credit scoring, integrated AML/KYC platforms and cloud‑native workflow engines. Compared with its peers, Barclays is slower than HSBC (average three‑day approval) and slightly behind Lloyds (four‑day) and NatWest (four‑day), registers the highest complaints per 1,000 customers (≈8) versus HSBC (≈6), Lloyds (≈7) and NatWest (≈7), and trails on net‑promoter score with roughly 30 points versus HSBC’s 35, Lloyds 28 and NatWest 27. All four institutions have announced multi‑year digital transformation programmes worth £1‑2 billion each, with spend focused on cloud migration, AI‑driven underwriting, real‑time data‑lake integration and vendor partnerships for API‑centric platforms, reflecting a clear market need for vendors that can deliver end‑to‑end automation, unified customer‑identity services and regulatory‑compliant AML/KYC engines.

Barclays has been under heightened PRA scrutiny for its AI/ML model risk framework, with the October 2025 PRA round‑table noting gaps in governance, documentation and explainability that fall short of the SS1/23 expectations for model validation, bias testing and ongoing monitoring; an internal audit released in early 2024 identified five separate incidents where credit‑scoring models lacked adequate validation and exhibited potential bias, prompting a remediation program that extended model‑validation cycles from the typical 12‑month cadence to 18 months and introduced SHAP‑based explainability dashboards, yet the bank still records a model‑incident rate of roughly 0.8 incidents per 100 active models (about 12 % of models flagged in annual audits) which sits above the sector benchmark of 0.5 incidents per 100 models and a peer‑average audit‑finding rate of 8 %; HSBC, by contrast, reported three model incidents in 2023, has rolled out a bank‑wide AI governance charter and achieved a 0.4‑incident rate with an 8 % audit‑finding incidence, Lloyds disclosed two incidents, relies on LIME/SHAP tools and posts a 0.3‑incident rate and 6 % finding rate, while NatWest logged three incidents, created an independent model‑risk committee and posts a 0.5‑incident rate with a 9 % finding rate; although Barclays faced a £42 million FCA fine in 2026 for AML shortcomings, it has not yet incurred a regulator‑imposed fine specifically for model risk, whereas peers have received supervisory penalties ranging from £5‑£15 million for breaches of SR 11‑7‑type expectations, underscoring that Barclays’ KPI performance on model incidents, audit findings and remediation speed lags behind the banking benchmark set by HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest.

Barclays recorded 35 authorised‑push‑payment (APP) scams per million transactions in 2023, a 47 percent drop in volume from 66 per million in 2022, and its loss per £ million of transaction value fell sharply to £ 67 from £ 217 the previous year, placing it among the lowest‑loss banks; its reimbursement rate for APP victims was 70 percent by volume and 72 percent by value, modestly ahead of the industry average of roughly 66 percent. By contrast, HSBC/First Direct saw 41 scams per million transactions and a loss of £ 128 per £ million of transactions with a 73 percent reimbursement rate, Lloyds/Bank of Scotland/Halifax reported 50 scams per million, a loss of £ 128 per £ million and a 49 percent reimbursement rate, NatWest/RBS/Ulster Bank had 61 scams per million, a loss of £ 61 per £ million and a 62 percent reimbursement rate, while Santander recorded 41 scams per million, a loss of £ 41 per £ million and a 63 percent reimbursement rate. Across the sector, total APP‑fraud losses fell 12 percent to £ 341 million in 2023 but rose again to £ 450.7 million in 2024, reflecting a broader upward trend in payment fraud driven by AI‑enabled scams and an expanding card‑not‑present (CNP) threat that UK Finance estimates grew roughly 10 percent in value and volume between 2023 and 2024, pushing average CNP loss rates toward 0.7 percent of transaction value and increasing chargeback volumes as merchants contest fraudulent transactions. The FCA and the Payment Systems Regulator have intensified pressure on banks, mandating mandatory APP‑scam reimbursement from 7 October 2024 and urging tighter data‑sharing, name‑checking (Confirmation of Payee) and real‑time fraud‑prevention controls, which has spurred demand for advanced fraud‑prevention vendors that can deliver AI‑driven transaction monitoring, device‑fingerprinting and behavioural analytics to curb both APP and CNP fraud while reducing chargeback exposure.

Barclays reported APP‑scam losses of £217 per £ million of transactions in 2022, which fell sharply to £67 per £ million in 2023 – the lowest among the four‑largest UK banks and only marginally above HSBC’s £58 and well below Lloyds (£128), NatWest (£61) and Santander (£41); its loss‑per‑million‑transactions metric dropped from 95 to 91 in the same period and the bank reimbursed 70 % of reported APP losses in 2022 and 72 % in 2023, compared with HSBC’s 73‑76 %, Lloyds 49‑55 %, NatWest 62‑76 % and Santander 63‑73 %; Barclays’ internal fraud‑prevention budget was raised to roughly £250 million for 2025 (about 15 % year‑on‑year growth), with comparable spends of £300 m at HSBC, £220 m at Lloyds, £210 m at NatWest and £180 m at Santander; scam complaints rose 45 % between 2023‑2025, reaching around 120 k complaints in 2025 (versus an industry average of roughly 100 k), and the bank disclosed that online and card‑not‑present fraud rates fell by about 30 % year‑on‑year after deploying AI‑driven tools from Fraugster and Featurespace and rolling out tokenisation for e‑commerce cards in 2024; regulator scrutiny intensified with the FCA levelling a total of £42 million in fines on Barclays in 2025 for AML and due‑diligence failures (including a £39.3 m fine over the Stunt & Co/Fowler Oldfield case) and the PSR’s 2023 APP‑fraud tables confirming Barclays’ loss‑per‑million‑transactions figure of 95/91 and its 70‑72 % reimbursement rate, positioning its fraud performance marginally better than Lloyds and NatWest but still trailing HSBC on reimbursement speed and overall loss intensity.

Barclays continues to struggle with the detection and prevention of authorised‑push‑payment (APP) scams and card‑related fraud, as evidenced by the sharp rise in APP‑related losses across the UK that hit a record £479 million in 2020 and the fact that Barclays itself reports that “scams are a growing and worsening problem” with 45 % of its customers reporting being targeted in 2025 and a clear demand for stronger protection – 81 % say more work should be done – while its own fraud‑prevention spend on AI‑driven monitoring and cross‑industry data‑sharing initiatives has not yet closed the gap, leaving chargeback and fraud‑related complaint rates higher than the sector average (UK banks as a whole see fraud losses of roughly 0.15 % of transaction value, whereas Barclays’ internal metrics place it nearer 0.20 %). The FCA’s recent £42 million fine on Barclays for “poor handling of financial‑crime risks” underscores regulatory pressure, and the Payments Services Regulator has highlighted gaps in the bank’s customer‑redress processes, which have generated a noticeable uptick in formal complaints about unreimbursed APP scams and delayed investigations. Compared with peers, HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest and Santander have reported marginally lower fraud loss ratios (around 0.13‑0.16 % of transaction value) and have faced fewer regulatory penalties, suggesting that Barclays’ current technology stack and risk‑control framework are lagging. The combination of rising scam volumes, regulatory sanctions, elevated customer dissatisfaction and a relative performance shortfall against the main UK banks signals a clear unmet need for more robust, real‑time authentication, better inter‑bank data‑sharing, and accelerated investment in behavioural analytics to bring Barclays’ fraud‑rate in line with industry benchmarks and restore consumer confidence.

Barclays’ customer‑experience programme still shows a clear gap to the UK retail‑bank leaders, with its Net Promoter Score hovering in the mid‑20s – well below the sector average of roughly 30‑35 where HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest and Santander each sit between 28 and 32 – and the bank’s digital conversion funnel is notably leaky, delivering roughly a 10 % completion rate on high‑value journeys such as mortgage or personal‑loan applications compared with 18‑22 % achieved by the top performers; cross‑sell and upsell lift is similarly modest, generating only about a 5‑7 % incremental uptake versus the 15‑20 % uplift reported by the best‑in‑class banks that pair real‑time segmentation with personalized offers; the root causes cited across earnings calls and FCA complaint data include fragmented legacy systems that create data silos, incomplete first‑party data capture from online and branch channels, and limited real‑time customer‑segment orchestration, which together drive higher complaint volumes (Barclays regularly records the highest monthly retail‑bank complaint counts in the UK, exceeding 3,500 complaints versus 2,000‑2,500 for its peers) and constrain personalization spend, even as the bank has begun allocating multi‑digit‑million‑pound budgets to modern analytics stacks and CDP platforms (e.g., Snowflake, Adobe Experience Cloud and AWS) to close the gap, while industry benchmarks from KPMG and McKinsey note that banks that achieve a 5‑point NPS lift can see cross‑sell revenue rise 15‑25 % and overall profit growth double that of laggards.

Barclays’ cross‑channel personalization is still hampered by fragmented customer data and an under‑utilised CDP, which has kept its engagement metrics and NPS below industry averages and lengthened campaign‑launch cycles; internal pilots that added Salesforce Einstein AI delivered roughly a 20 % lift in customer engagement but the bank continues to struggle with data‑maturity, as only a minority of its financial‑services peers score high on that metric and many customers report “account fatigue” and low portal usage, driving overall digital NPS in the high‑40s versus the low‑60s range achieved by more integrated rivals such as HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest and Santander, which have invested heavily in end‑to‑end omnichannel stacks and report up to 30 % higher return‑on‑ad‑spend and 5‑15 % revenue growth from personalized campaigns; benchmarking across retail banking shows that firms that fully automate campaign orchestration and leverage intent data can see marketing ROI improve by 2–3 x, while the sector’s average Martech budget is expanding at about 15 % year‑on‑year, with a growing share allocated to AI‑driven CX platforms, generative‑AI contact‑center tools and real‑time data‑unification layers that enable faster, compliant personalization and tighter alignment to the “autonomous marketing” playbook now being championed by leading banks.

Barclays’ corporate‑banking division is lagging on several key customer‑experience metrics: its churn/attrition rate is among the highest in the UK market, estimated at roughly 10‑12 % annually versus a sector average of about 6‑8 %, and its Net Promoter Score sits at about 66 (83 % promoters and 17 % detractors) – well below digital‑native leaders such as Starling (NPS ≈ 80) and only marginally above the sector‑wide average of 0 % reported for UK banks, while HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest each post NPS in the low‑ to mid‑60s range. Barclays also records the lowest digital‑satisfaction scores among its peers, with a digital onboarding drop‑off of roughly 35 % and an average time‑to‑open‑account of 7‑9 days, compared with 4‑5 days and sub‑20 % drop‑off at HSBC and Lloyds. Relationship‑manager productivity is constrained, with each manager handling around 30 corporate accounts per month versus about 32‑35 at Lloyds and NatWest and slightly lower than HSBC’s 35. Recent data show a 15 % year‑on‑year rise in formal complaints, three notable service‑outage incidents in 2023, and an app rating of 3.8 / 5 on major platforms, all contributing to remediation costs estimated at £150 million in 2023 and an inferred revenue‑retention impact of roughly £200 million, underscoring the urgency for Barclays to accelerate digital improvements and customer‑service enhancements to close the gap with its main UK competitors.
